newsitem.title: UK: Gilts slip, demand wanes as UK Labour romps ahead.
newsitem.headline: Gilts slip, demand wanes as UK Labour romps ahead.

text.p: British gilts crept up, then retraced their gains on Friday morning after early indications of a landslide majority for the opposition Labour party in the country's elections.

The 10-year benchmark cash gilt rose as high as 99-07 from 98-27 before initial exit polls pointed to majority of more than 150 seats in the 659-seat parliament for Labour. By 0002 GMT they were at 98-23 to yield 7.42 percent.
Dealers said the pullback in gilts was largely due to thin trade and lack of follow-through buying as traders went home early after the initial excitement had died down.

"The market seems reasonably comfortable with the way things are going at the moment. There's nothing really in the move down -- there was some buying interest earlier but no follow through," said one dealer.
Traders said the market would likely settle around present levels, as long as the results that filtered in were in line with the exit polls.
"After the first flurry, prices seem to have slowed down," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
"If some of the later seats confirm that the exit poll wasn't far from the truth, we could settle down around current levels."
Salesmen at J.P.Morgan said the curve had flattened with trade concentrated in swaps. They said the outlook for gilts was partly contingent on the course of sterling.
Sterling also pared its early gains, with the rate against the mark returning to around its pre-exit poll level. By 2331 GMT sterling/mark was at 2.7965/75.
The 25-year cash gilt was at 104-23 to yield 7.57 percent after rising as high as 105-08 earlier.

The 10-year gilt spread with Bunds -- which were not trading -- was at 178 basis points, down from 183 basis points before the results started to come in but up from 177 basis points immediately after initial exit polls.
J.P.Morgan said a move to 170 basis points on the spread would likely trigger some profit taking.

DKB International chief economist Gerard Lyons said the gilt market was unlikely to do much initially, but added yields would likely trend down as inflation under a possible Labour government remains low.
"There won't be any dramatic shift in policy, just an endorsement of the tough fiscal stance and a commitment to tackle inflation by raising interest rates," said Lyons.
"I think they'll do that at the next monetary policy meeting...but I still don't think rates will go up as much as the market is expecting. I think they will go up in two quarter point moves."
The short sterling strip is discounting a 50 basis point rate rise by June and a further 25 basis point rise by September. British base rates are currently at 6.0 percent.
